card.hook: Two pale towers rise over Quito's colonial rooftops, and a local legend says the world ends the day this church is finished. Good news: it's still described as unfinished, so you've got time.
card.stand_here: Head to El Panecillo, the hill to the south, and face north across the historic centre. The twin towers and south façade rise above the rooftops, with the hill's Virgin statue in the foreground.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to bring the towers closer. Switch to 1x when you want the Virgin statue and the whole skyline in the shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the towers on one of the vertical lines, and let the rooftops fill the lower third.
card.best_time: One guide recommends sunrise, or after dark when the building is lit. After dark, try night mode.
card.selfie_here: Go to the open plaza in front of the main façade and stand back from the entrance, so the full height of the towers rises behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and use its wider option if your phone has one.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone at the corner where Calle Venezuela meets Calle Carchi, ask them to hold it low and tilt it up so both towers fit against the sky, and step into the frame in front of them.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship and the tower climb is ticketed, so check the official site for visiting arrangements. Guides describe the climb's narrow wooden bridge and steep ladders as nerve-wracking, so walk the outer ledges carefully.
card.challenge: Catch a corner of the Virgin statue and both towers in one shot, so it looks like she's keeping an eye on the basilica.
card.good_to_know: Father Julio Matovelle came up with the idea in 1883, as a reminder of Ecuador's consecration to the Sacred Heart. The first stone was laid in 1892 and the basilica was consecrated in 1988. It reaches 83 m, and the crypt holds the National Pantheon of Ecuador.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to El Panecillo, the hill to the south, and face north across the historic centre. The twin towers and south façade rise above the rooftops, with the hill's Virgin statue in the foreground.

card.hook: You step out of the gondola and Quito is stretched along the valley below you, with Andean volcanoes standing behind it if the sky is feeling generous. It's a big view, so give yourself a minute to take it in.
card.stand_here: Stand at the main railing at the Cruz Loma lookout beside the upper station. Face out over the railing so the city fills the valley below you and the volcanoes sit behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the wide view over the city, then try 0.5x to squeeze in the volcanoes and plenty of sky. Want the gondola cabins on the slope? Try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line so the city gets most of the frame, then use the railing or the edge of the upper station as a foreground.
card.best_time: Weekday mornings, roughly 9:00 to 11:00, are your best bet: the sky is usually clearest and it's least crowded. Fog can still drift in, so check the weather before you ride, because afternoon cloud often hides the volcanoes.
card.selfie_here: Walk a short way from the top station along the trail toward the highest lookout and take your selfie on the swing, so it looks like you're floating over Quito (go before the crowds build). For a dramatic one, try the Bridge in the Clouds, the walkway outside the cafe beside the top station, with the station area over your shoulder. Use the front camera, and switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it.
card.rules_and_safety: At around 4,000 meters the air is thin and breathing can be hard for some people, so take it easy and let yourself settle in before you start shooting. A photo ID is needed to buy a lift ticket, and you must keep the stub for the return.
card.challenge: Catch a gondola cabin with the whole city blurred softly behind it: zoom in on a cabin, tap it, and let Quito do the rest.
card.good_to_know: The TelefériQo opened in July 2005 and is one of the highest aerial lifts in the world, rising from 3,117 m to 3,945 m. The ride takes about twenty minutes. Up top you'll find a public restroom, a small cafe and a few shops, and it's cooler and windier than in the city.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the main railing at the Cruz Loma lookout beside the upper station. Face out over the railing so the city fills the valley below you and the volcanoes sit behind it.

card.hook: You can spot her from much of Quito, but nothing beats standing right beside those aluminium wings with the whole old town spread out behind you.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Mirador del Panecillo, the viewing platform inside the base of the statue, which you reach by the stairs in the monument. The statue is to the north-west of you, so face that way to get her whole figure with room to step back.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x when you're close, so her wings and base fit in one frame. Switch to 1x for the city views, then try 2x or 5x for her face, her wings or the faraway volcanoes (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky or the city, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky keeps its colour and the statue doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Sunset and blue hour, when the city lights come on, are the most recommended. For fewer crowds, some guides prefer early morning. If you stay for the lights, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep your phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the foot of the Virgin, just past the small ticket booth, and take your selfie there in the late-afternoon light for a warm glow. Use the front camera, hold it up high and tilt it a little so she towers over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the base of the statue and ask a passer-by to shoot upward from the ground in front of you, or from one side, at zoom 0.5x so her full figure fits in.
card.rules_and_safety: Take a taxi or app ride up and back rather than walking, because the walk up the hill has a real mugging history. The platform inside the base is paid; the fee is reported to be small but may have changed, so check on the day.
card.challenge: Fill the whole frame with her wings and sky, then take a second shot of the same wings with the city tucked underneath, and see which one you like better.
card.good_to_know: At 41 metres including the base, she's the tallest statue in Ecuador and the tallest aluminium statue in the world. She was built from 7,400 numbered aluminium pieces, shipped over and put together on the hilltop, and finished on 28 March 1975. She's a giant version of the Virgin of Quito, a small wooden sculpture carved by Bernardo de Legarda in 1734.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Mirador del Panecillo, the viewing platform inside the base of the statue, which you reach by the stairs in the monument. The statue is to the north-west of you, so face that way to get her whole figure with room to step back.

selfie_spots.why: Late-afternoon light at the base is the setting these guides recommend, so a selfie taken there would likely catch that warm glow.

card.hook: Four grand buildings, one big open square, and you can fit them all in a single photo. Plaza de la Independencia is a great place to practise framing a whole scene instead of just one monument.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map in the northwest part of Plaza de la Independencia. Turn to look southeast and you'll see the square with the palaces all around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the whole square. Then switch to 1x for a calmer shot of one side, and zoom in (2x or 5x, depending on your phone) for details on the façades.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and keep the phone level, so the building edges stay straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning. The light is soft, and you'll get cleaner, emptier frames before the crowds and street vendors fill the square.
card.selfie_here: Take it out in the open square itself, with the plaza behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x so more of the scene fits over your shoulder, and aim for early morning when it's quiet.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the square while facing the Carondelet Palace on the north side, with you in front of the palace. That works well for a palace photo, but it won't catch the whole plaza.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is a free, open public space. Going inside the cathedral or the palaces isn't covered here.
card.challenge: Can you get the cathedral, the Carondelet Presidential Palace, the Archbishop's Palace and the Municipal Palace into one frame? Count them out loud to check.
card.good_to_know: The cathedral, the Carondelet Presidential Palace, the Archbishop's Palace and the Municipal Palace all face onto this plaza. For a second photo, walk to the southern side and frame the Archbishop's Palace with the open space and benches in front.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon on the map in the northwest part of Plaza de la Independencia. Turn to look southeast and you'll see the square with the palaces all around it.

card.hook: Here's a fun surprise: Quito's cathedral turns its long white side to the square, like it's ignoring you. A deep ravine blocked the grand front when it was built, so the belltower entrance sits around the corner on Calle García Moreno.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de la Independencia (Plaza Grande), in the northeast part of the square, facing the cathedral's arched entrance, with the cathedral to the west. You'll see the white wall and the arch, with the plaza and its central monument in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole side of the cathedral across the square. If you're close, zoom 0.5x gets the parapet and arch into one frame. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the Carondelet Arch, the belltower and the green domes.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep the stone parapet along the lower third so the building doesn't look tilted. Then tap the white wall and slide it a little darker so the paint keeps its detail against the sky.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the white walls than the middle of the day. One guide also suggests around 11:00 a.m. for good photo light, so you have a few options.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the paved square in front of the Carondelet Arch and its curved staircase. Use the front camera, and if it has a zoom 0.5x option, use it to fit more in. Face away from the arch and let it and the stairs fill the frame behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the open square across from the curved staircase and the Carondelet Arch, so the whole side of the cathedral fits in the frame, while you stand with the arch behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The plaza is an open public square, but the cathedral is an active place of worship. Sources disagree on photos inside, so check the signs or ask staff before you take your phone out. The rooftop and dome climb is paid, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you fit a stone sphere from the parapet in the foreground and the green domes and belltower peeking over the roofline in the same shot?
card.good_to_know: The cathedral has served as a cathedral since the 1540s and was consecrated in 1572. In 1995 it became the Cathedral of Ecuador, the senior Catholic church in the country. It has been repaired after several earthquakes and a volcanic eruption, so what you see is the result of many rebuildings.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza de la Independencia (Plaza Grande), in the northeast part of the square, facing the cathedral's arched entrance, with the cathedral to the west. You'll see the white wall and the arch, with the plaza and its central monument in front of you.

card.hook: On a weekend in La Carolina, you've got football, basketball, ecua-volley and kites all going at once, with a wall of city towers standing behind the lot. It's too big to shoot all at once, so pick one scene and let the rest be background.
card.stand_here: Stand at the start of the perimeter loop, just after the parking lot, and face north into the park. You'll get the big monumental cross in front of you, the green edge of the park, and a view toward the financial district towers from the loop.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the open lawns and a big sense of space, and 1x for most scenes with people and paths. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out kites or players without walking over.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line, so the grass and the sky both get some room.
card.best_time: Weekends are livelier, with games and kites, so they're best if you want people in the shot. For softer light and fewer harsh shadows, go in the morning or late afternoon.
card.selfie_here: Pose beside the retired Douglas DC-6 plane near the main entrance. It's the park's signature photo prop. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold the phone out a bit and get the plane behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: One guide praises the park for being safe and clean, and another mentions police on horseback. Before you go, check the official site for events, closures or rules covering the exhibition centre, botanical gardens and vivarium in the western part.
card.challenge: Catch a kite against the sky, then add two or three people at the bottom of the frame so everyone can see how big the park is.
card.good_to_know: The park covers about 165 acres (670,000 square metres) and grew from a farm that was taken over in 1939. In 1985 Pope John Paul II led a large open-air Catholic mass here, and a giant Christian cross was built to mark the place. Quiteños come mostly at weekends to play, run, fly kites and snack.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the start of the perimeter loop, just after the parking lot, and face north into the park. You'll get the big monumental cross in front of you, the green edge of the park, and a view toward the financial district towers from the loop.

card.hook: Picture a whole village tipping down a steep hillside, with a church dome sitting right in the middle like a cherry on a cake. That's Guápulo, and the best view is from above.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Mirador de Guápulo, at Larrea and Pasaje Stübel, on the hilltop above the village. Face south-east on the map, where the church and its dome sit below you with the Cumbayá valley and hills behind.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the church, the village roofs and the valley into one frame. Then tap 2x for a tighter shot of the dome, or 5x if your phone has it. Use 0.5x only for the whole valley, because the church will look small.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the dome on one of the lower crossing points and keep the horizon level, then tap the church and slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon gives lovely light on the church, and sunrise or sunset are good too. Go in daylight either way, as it's the sensible choice here.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Guápulo Mirador, on the lookout behind Hotel Quito beside the Francisco de Orellana statue. It's the one spot where the church sits in the valley below you, so use the front camera and keep the domes over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Down on the plaza at the bottom of the cobbled road from Hotel Quito, ask a passer-by to take your picture with the church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The mirador has been reported closed, so check it's open before you set off. Some visitors mention robberies and sketchy surroundings there, so keep your phone close and stick to daylight. Ask staff before taking photos inside the church.
card.challenge: Get the dome sitting neatly on a gridline crossing, then take a second shot where the volcanoes sneak into the background on a clear day.
card.good_to_know: Guápulo has a reputation as Quito's artsy, bohemian corner, with local artists and a few laid-back cafés and bars. The Spaniards originally founded it as an independent city. Every year on 7 September the Fiestas de Guápulo bring costumes, a parade, music and fireworks.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Mirador de Guápulo, at Larrea and Pasaje Stübel, on the hilltop above the village. Face south-east on the map, where the church and its dome sit below you with the Cumbayá valley and hills behind.

card.hook: Picture a big, bold, simple building sitting above Quito with the whole city and sky behind it. That's La Capilla del Hombre, and it's made for photos.
card.stand_here: Stand right at La Capilla del Hombre in Bellavista, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the building so its walls and a strip of sky both fit in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole building and its setting. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details in the walls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the walls straight, then tap a mid-tone patch of wall and slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go for soft morning or late-afternoon light. It's kinder to the walls and gives the sky more colour than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Head to the terraced courtyard just outside the chapel exit, the first spot you reach as you leave the building. Turn to face the city with the chapel at your back, switch to your front camera and try 0.5x to squeeze more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the terrace of the Casa Museo Guayasamín, across from the chapel, so they can get the full building in front of them with you posing at the chapel.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules inside the museum can differ from the outside, so check the official site before you go. It's a museum, so expect tickets and set visiting times.
card.challenge: Take one dead-level shot where the lines of the walls meet the sky, then another with a person beside the wall to show how big it really is.
card.good_to_know: La Capilla del Hombre means "The Chapel of Man" and is dedicated to the peoples of Latin America. The painter Oswaldo Guayasamín designed it with Handel Guayasamín. Building began in 1995 and finished in 2002, after the painter's death.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at La Capilla del Hombre in Bellavista, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the building so its walls and a strip of sky both fit in the frame.

selfie_spots.why: A guide describes this courtyard as overlooking the city and says it is the first thing you reach on leaving the building, which makes it a natural spot for a view with the chapel behind you.

card.hook: Picture a huge stone church at the top of a curving flight of steps, with a wide cobbled square laid out in front of it like a welcome mat. That's San Francisco, and it's a lot of church to fit on one phone screen.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de San Francisco, at the far eastern edge, about 30–40 m back from the church entrance. Face the church and you get the full stone facade with the open plaza leading up to it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade and the square in one shot. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved stonework and the towers.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the pale stonework, then slide it a little darker so the sky and carvings keep their detail.
card.best_time: Sunrise to about 8am is the sweet spot: the square is emptier and the early light falls right on the carving. Late afternoon is also suggested for golden light.
card.selfie_here: Climb the stone steps of the atrio, the raised forecourt in front of the church, and turn so your back is to the church with the plaza in front of you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the church fill in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the far eastern edge of the square, about 30 to 40 metres from the church entrance, while you pose out in the open plaza in front of the facade.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally not allowed inside the church, so take all your pictures outside. Pickpocketing can happen in crowded tourist areas around the church, so keep an eye on your belongings while you pose.
card.challenge: Grab a shot with a few cobbles at the bottom so they lead your eye straight up the steps to the towers.
card.good_to_know: This is described as the oldest and most significant religious site in Ecuador. It's also the largest architectural complex in any historic centre in South America, at about three and a half hectares. Work on the current building started in 1550, finished around 1680, and it was officially inaugurated in 1705.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza de San Francisco, at the far eastern edge, about 30–40 m back from the church entrance. Face the church and you get the full stone facade with the open plaza leading up to it.

card.hook: Picture a narrow cobbled lane where every balcony, lantern and painted wall leans in and points you down the street. La Ronda is basically a phone-camera cheat code.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle Juan de Dios Morales, known as La Ronda, at the western end, and look back along the lane. It is about 768 m south-east of the street's mapped position, so the street is to the north-west of where you stand.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the facades and balconies, and switch on the gridlines so the walls stay straight. Then try zoom 0.5x to fit in more balconies, or zoom 2x to squeeze the lantern-lined houses together.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a sunlit wall, then slide the brightness down a little to make it darker, so the bright paint keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into early evening, when the low warm sun lights up the painted walls.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the lane near its western end with the painted facades behind you, using the front camera, in late afternoon or early evening light. After dark, stay on the main pedestrian lane under the string lights for a glowing backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: Photographing the street and buildings is generally fine, but ask before taking close-ups of people, especially performers. Keep a firm grip on your phone and watch for anyone who gets too close. Shops and restaurants along the lane may have their own rules, so check the signs.
card.challenge: Let the cobbles run into the bottom corner of your shot, put the lanterns down one side, and wait for a gap in the crowd. Bonus points if you catch it with no one in the frame.
card.good_to_know: La Ronda is a narrow cobbled lane in central Quito. Its official name on the map is Calle Juan de Dios Morales, but locals call it La Ronda. You'll see colourful colonial-style facades, balconies and lanterns all the way along.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Calle Juan de Dios Morales, known as La Ronda, at the western end, and look back along the lane. It is about 768 m south-east of the street's mapped position, so the street is to the north-west of where you stand.

card.hook: The front of La Compañía is solid grey volcanic stone, and it's carved so densely that you'll stand there picking out plants and symbols you missed the first time. Inside it's all gold leaf, which is how it got the nickname "Temple of Solomon of South America".
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right by the church on the corner of García Moreno and Sucre streets. Face the stone façade, and step back a little so the whole front fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the tall façade in from close up, then 1x for a natural view of the doorway. Try 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to fill the frame with the carved stone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the façade with the vertical lines, and keep the phone level so the stonework doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is the recommended time for softer light on the stone. Check the official site for visiting times.
card.selfie_here: Try the raised terrace in front of the San Francisco church on Plaza San Francisco, where La Compañía's dome shows in the view. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the dome behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by in the plaza in front of the church to frame the whole façade with you in it, and check the plaza's spot on the map first.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography rules may apply inside and the sources disagree, so check the official site before you go. Dress respectfully and be considerate of people who are praying.
card.challenge: Find one carved plant in the stonework and get a close-up where the stone fills the whole screen.
card.good_to_know: The Jesuits reached Quito in 1586, and the church took roughly 160 years to build. The stone façade was finished on 24 July 1765. It's mostly Baroque but mixes four styles, and Pope John Paul II (1985) and Pope Francis (2015) have both visited.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right by the church on the corner of García Moreno and Sucre streets. Face the stone façade, and step back a little so the whole front fits.

card.hook: Step onto the terrace in front of the church and look south. A hotel dome sits right in front of a whole hill, and it looks like Quito arranged it for you.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, on the terrace in front of the Church of St. Francis in Plaza de San Francisco, and face south across the plaza. The dome of the Casa Gangotena will be in front of you, with El Panecillo behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full terrace view. Try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out El Panecillo and the dome. For the church front, walk east down into the plaza and use zoom 0.5x to fit it all in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the dome and the hill on separate lines so they don't merge into one blob.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is a good bet, because the sun sets over the church and the distant Pichincha volcano. One guide prefers sunrise, so try both if you're staying nearby.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the open cobbled plaza with the church towers rising right behind you, away from the entrance. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if yours has it, and keep the towers over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand at the far eastern edge of the plaza, about 30 to 40 metres from the church entrance, while you stand in the plaza in front of the facade so the full church is in frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos aren't allowed inside the church, so keep your shots to the plaza and the outside. Keep an eye on your surroundings and belongings while you line up the picture.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the dome and El Panecillo sit on their own gridlines, then another with a few tiny people crossing the square to show how big the church is.
card.good_to_know: The square is named after the Church and Convent of St. Francis, whose whitewashed front fills one side. Around it you'll find the Chapel of Villacís, the Chapel of Cantuña and the Casa Gangotena on a corner. The plaza is built on ancient Incan ruins, including the palace of Emperor Atahualpa.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, on the terrace in front of the Church of St. Francis in Plaza de San Francisco, and face south across the plaza. The dome of the Casa Gangotena will be in front of you, with El Panecillo behind it.

card.hook: You step into a 17th-century colonial house, and a few rooms later a carved face is looking straight back at you. It's an old house and ancient objects in one stop, so your camera roll will be busy.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map. That's Casa del Alabado itself, so you shoot from inside its courtyards and rooms rather than from far away. Start in a courtyard facing the house walls, then head indoors for the objects.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x in the courtyards to fit the house and a strip of sky. Switch to 1x for rooms and display cases, and 2x or more for object details when you can't get closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the object, then slide the brightness down a touch to make it darker so lit pieces don't wash out, and keep the flash off.
card.best_time: Go during opening hours, and pick a time when the daylight in the courtyards feels soft. Quieter moments are easier for object shots with nobody in the frame. If the rooftop terrace is open when you visit, sunset is named as the best time to shoot up there.
card.selfie_here: Try the central courtyard near the fountain, if it's still there when you visit. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the greenery and the colonial walls behind you. If you can get up to the terrace, put the museum building and the historic-centre skyline over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement of Calle Cuenca, opposite the entrance gate, and frame the street-side facade and gate with you in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Non-flash photography for personal use is generally allowed and flash is typically prohibited inside, so check the posted signs and the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Fill the whole frame with one curved vessel or carved face, with no other visitors in the shot, and see if it looks like a museum postcard.
card.good_to_know: Casa del Alabado is a Pre-Columbian art museum in a colonial house built in the 17th century. It has two courtyards, eight exhibit rooms and a shop. About 500 of its 5,000-plus archaeological pieces are on permanent display, arranged by theme like cosmology, ancestors, ritual and the natural world.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map. That's Casa del Alabado itself, so you shoot from inside its courtyards and rooms rather than from far away. Start in a courtyard facing the house walls, then head indoors for the objects.

card.hook: Picture giant letters spelling QUITO, with the whole old centre and the Basílica lined up behind them like they're posing too. That's the Itchimbía photo, and it says where you are in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand in Parque Itchimbía, near the big 'Quito' letters on the hilltop. Face the city, with the letters low in front of you and the historic centre behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the letters and the city in one go. Try 1x for a more natural look, then 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Basílica.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the horizon on the upper third line, and tap the letters so they stay nice and sharp.
card.best_time: Early morning is your best bet for a clear view across the city and towards the nearby volcanoes. Midday can look flat, so skip it if you can.
card.selfie_here: Squeeze into or next to the 'Q' of the big QUITO letters, with the city behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit low so the letters and the skyline both fit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Park entry is free, but check the official site before you go, especially for the Centro Cultural Itchimbía. Reviewers describe the park as safe, with security patrols and a family-friendly feel, especially on weekends. The hilltop is open and breezy, so bring a light layer.
card.challenge: Get the letters, the Basílica and your own grin in one frame, then crouch a little and see if the letters get even bigger.
card.good_to_know: Itchimbía is a hill on the eastern edge of downtown Quito, with a park on top. The glass-walled Centro Cultural Itchimbía up there holds an exhibition centre, a conference room and a museum. It makes a great second photo: step back a few paces so the whole building fits, and let the city show through the glass.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Parque Itchimbía, near the big 'Quito' letters on the hilltop. Face the city, with the letters low in front of you and the historic centre behind them.

card.hook: Walk up to the corner of Calle Chile and Calle Guayaquil and the church just faces you, head-on, with the carved portal and the tall bell tower stacked in one frame. For a phone, it's about as friendly as a building gets.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Calle Chile and Calle Guayaquil, the corner where the church sits, and face the facade. The street is tight, so step back to the kerb or the opposite pavement to fit the tower in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole facade and tower in from the pavement, then go to 1x for a more natural look. Use zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the carved portal and the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean, and tap the facade and slide a bit darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the sun is high enough to light the facade instead of leaving it in shadow. Early in the day usually means fewer people on the pavement, but check the light when you get there.
card.selfie_here: Head to Plaza Huerto San Agustín, in the plaza behind the convent, and pose beside the life-size bronze Augustinian priest, which a local guide says draws lots of selfies. Use the front camera, and check on the spot whether the church makes it into your frame, because it may not.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Calle Mejía, facing the church and Calle Guayaquil, while you pose in front of the church. It's a rough spot, so shuffle a little until the church fits.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship, so dress modestly. Keep the flash off inside, especially during a service, and check the official site for which parts of the convent are open.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the tower is perfectly straight against your gridlines, then one where you try to make it lean on purpose from Calle Mejía. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The Augustinians were given this site in 1573 and built the convent first. The church followed between 1606 and 1617, to plans by Francisco Becerra. The bell tower is 37 metres tall and still holds its 17th-century bells, and the convent's Chapter House is where the Act of the Governing Board of 1809 was signed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Calle Chile and Calle Guayaquil, the corner where the church sits, and face the facade. The street is tight, so step back to the kerb or the opposite pavement to fit the tower in.

card.hook: This building is about 162 m across, so if you stand too close, your phone just gives up and shows you a wall. Back up, take a breath and let the whole plain, solid frontage fill the frame.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon on the map, right at the Centro Cultural Metropolitano itself. Walk to the edge of the building, then step back as far as the pavement lets you and face the facade.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x with the gridlines on for your main shot. If the pavement is too narrow, switch to zoom 0.5x to fit more building and street, but keep the phone level or the walls will lean. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is great for doorways, windows and carved stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edge of the facade with an upright grid line so the walls stay straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the street. If you want the rooftop, go in daylight.
card.selfie_here: Try the rooftop terrace of the Centro Cultural Metropolitano, reached from inside the building. Use the front camera, and switch to 0.5x to squeeze in more of the city behind you. Your backdrop here is the city, not the building, so check the framing before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by at the corner of García Moreno and Espejo, by the main entrance, and stand a few steps back on the pavement so the facade fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography for personal use is generally allowed in most areas, but check for restrictions in specific exhibitions. Entry may be restricted and sources disagree on whether the roof is open, so check the official site or ask locally before you go.
card.challenge: Take one big 'whole building' shot, then one close-up of a single doorway or window. Can you make them look like they're from two different trips?
card.good_to_know: The building dates back to 1622 and has been a cultural institution since 1997. Before that it housed the First Central University, and it was also a jail where Spanish authorities executed insurgents during the Ecuadorian War of Independence. The facade was rebuilt in the 20th century, so what you see from the street is a mix of eras.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the phone icon on the map, right at the Centro Cultural Metropolitano itself. Walk to the edge of the building, then step back as far as the pavement lets you and face the facade.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where the visitor stands with the building directly behind them, so the selfie spot is the roof terrace, which is a stated photo spot but its backdrop is the city rather than the building. The ask-someone spot is the corner of García Moreno and Espejo, which pages name as the main entrance; the advice to stand on the pavement there is my own inference, not from a source. No page mentions selfie sticks. The roof terrace's opening hours are not stated; one source notes the rooftop is best in daylight. Sources disagree on whether the building is open on the roof, so check locally before visiting.

card.hook: Quito's Historic Center is a busy jumble, and then there's this bright white church with its square tower and five domes, standing out like it's wearing its Sunday best.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de la Merced, the open square in front of the church, and face the façade. The church is to the north, about 1 minute on foot, so walk across the square towards the entrance.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole façade, tower and square into one frame. Then try 1x for a tidier view, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the tower and the decoration.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white walls, then drag the slider a touch darker so they keep their detail instead of washing out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives gentler light on the white walls. Go early for fewer people in the square, and expect crowds and festivities around the feast of the Virgin on 24 September.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and turn around so the white church is over your shoulder. Try 0.5x if your phone offers it on the front camera, so the tower fits in behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the open square from the façade, on the Calle Chile side, so the whole church and tower fit in the frame, while you stand with the church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship and photography inside is generally not allowed, so plan on exterior shots only. Check locally for visiting arrangements.
card.challenge: Catch someone crossing the square towards the entrance, with the whole tower in the frame and standing straight against a gridline.
card.good_to_know: This was the first church and headquarters of the Mercedarian Order in Ecuador, which is why it's a basilica. Building began in 1701, the tower was finished in 1736 and the church was consecrated in 1737. Look closely at the decoration for Inca and Arabic-style inscriptions.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza de la Merced, the open square in front of the church, and face the façade. The church is to the north, about 1 minute on foot, so walk across the square towards the entrance.

ask_someone_spot.name: Plaza de La Merced, the open square in front of the church facade (Calle Chile side)
ask_someone_spot.detail: Stand across the open square from the white facade so the whole church, including the tower, fits in frame. Calle Chile runs past the church.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where the visitor stands with the basilica directly behind them, so I returned no selfie spots rather than guess. The square in front of the church is named as a good backdrop for a photo of someone, which is why it is the passer-by spot. The Casa Gangotena rooftop and the El Panecillo viewpoint show the basilica among other churches or in the middle ground, but no page says a visitor should stand there with the basilica behind them, so I left them out. The basilica tower climb is named for views over the city, but it does not put the church behind the visitor. The square's name is taken from a Wikimedia file title, and the Plaza de La Merced name is not confirmed by a page describing the square itself. The church's listed street address is Calle Chile or Cuenca, which the sources give inconsistently. Check the exact square on the map before sending visitors.
